tldr: Mind readers: a Mandarin speech implant gave a woman with ALS her voice back, a ring sensed stress, a quick test plus a blood test flagged Alzheimer's, and AI designed a drug that worked in mice.
window: Window: the 24 hours to 06:20 AEDT, Sat 28 Nov 2026.
notes: This week: Tencent and Monash's Nature paper (25 Nov), the 'AI stroke' study (26 Nov) and the fingerprint blood-type papers (Retraction Watch, 23 Nov).

Evidence: the speech implant is one patient in an early trial, reported by the hospital; the ring is a six-person test; the drug, NAD+ and killifish results are in mice and fish; the psilocybin figures pool six small trials; the aged-care and Alzheimer's-screening studies are observational analyses; Peter Gabriel's is an opinion and Q.ANT's a company account.
Screenshots are the publishers' public pages as captured on 28 Nov 2026; copyright remains with the publishers.

stories.title: A wireless Mandarin speech implant gave a woman with ALS her voice back, in an early trial
stories.summary: At Huashan Hospital in Shanghai, two 256-channel electrode arrays turn a woman's attempted speech into Chinese characters at about 80 a minute, over 95% right, voiced in a clone of her own voice; imagined speech topped 90% at about 110 a minute. One participant so far, reported by the hospital and team.

predictions.note: A wireless implant restored speech for one woman with ALS in an early trial: a step for implantable interfaces, far from two-way symbiosis.

stories.title: A USC smart ring sensed stress from fingertip sweat about 92% of the time, in a tiny test
stories.summary: Two infrared LEDs spot sweat before it beads, and with pulse, temperature and an on-board AI the ring told rest from ice-water stress about 92% of the time in six volunteers, against 78% for a gel sensor. Next up: 40 office workers over a year, a step toward wearables that notice stress early.

stories.title: Tencent and Monash's AI designed a drug that beat Wegovy's ingredient in mice at a tenth the dose
stories.summary: A Nature paper from Tencent, China's SIAT and Australia's Monash University: its open-source AI, ORIDTP, designed peptides that hit two targets at once, and one gave obese mice more weight loss than semaglutide at a tenth of the dose over 21 days. It is preclinical, and the authors say it is not evidence it is clinically superior.

predictions.note: Tencent's AI-designed drug candidates worked in mice, a preclinical step that is years from any regulator's approval.

stories.title: Scientists gave an AI a mock stroke, and its word slips echoed stroke survivors'
stories.summary: A University of South Carolina team damaged layers of an open vision-language model and gave it the language tests used with stroke patients; sorting its errors predicted the brain damage behind similar slips in people. Neurology's toolkit may help explain why AIs fail.

stories.title: In a UK first, an AI agent paid for nine pizzas straight from a bank account
stories.summary: In the Financial Conduct Authority's sandbox, Papa John's AI agent ordered nine mini pizzas and paid bank to bank through Lloyds and TrueLayer, with spending capped per order and per month and no card or account details shared. A glimpse of agents running errands for us.

stories.title: Peter Gabriel: if we can't beat AI, join it, by uploading superintelligence into our brains
stories.summary: The former Genesis frontman, 76, told The Sun he is very concerned about AI's military uses but excited by its promise for medicine and abundance, and that we need to look at 'uploading superintelligence into our brains or our future cyborg selves.' An opinion, not a plan.

stories.title: A quick tablet test plus a blood test could spare most memory patients a brain scan
stories.summary: In 1,001 US adults aged 60-85, a 3-minute iPad clock-and-recall test or a 10-minute computer test, followed by a blood test for amyloid, detected Alzheimer's while letting over 60% skip formal memory testing and up to 85% of people with memory problems skip a PET scan. Easier, earlier checks for dementia.

stories.title: Live fast, live long: fertile male killifish outlived their peers
stories.summary: At Germany's Leibniz Institute on Aging, male turquoise killifish that fathered more when young lived longer on average, against the idea that early reproduction costs lifespan. One shared biological 'quality' may drive both, so health and fertility may share roots. Untested in females, other species or people.

stories.title: One way of boosting NAD+, a molecule longevity pills chase, thinned old mice's bones
stories.summary: Mice lacking CD38, an enzyme that uses up NAD+, had about five times the bone NAD+ in old age, yet thinner spine and leg bones as bone breakdown sped up. Raising NAD+ another way left bone markers more youthful: a reminder to target the right tissue. A gene knockout in mice, not a supplement.

stories.title: 72% of older Australians changed doctors on moving into a nursing home
stories.summary: The Registry of Senior Australians found that of about 41,000 people entering residential aged care, 72% changed their usual primary care provider, against about 10% of those starting care at home. Continuity came back after the move; better handovers would help keep care joined up as Australia ages.

stories.title: Pooling six small trials, psilocybin therapy nearly tripled the odds of staying off alcohol
stories.summary: A review of six modern trials with 202 adults with alcohol use disorder found moderate short-term drops in drinking with psilocybin plus therapy, and in the three randomised trials nearly three times the odds of abstinence 4 to 28 weeks on (definitions varied). Side effects were mostly mild; the authors call the evidence early and mixed.

stories.title: Kyoto scientists may have found the brain's dream-sleep switch
stories.summary: An MRI atlas built from 10 donated brainstems, then scans of 98 people with REM sleep behaviour disorder and 114 healthy adults, pointed to a small nucleus that may be the human REM sleep centre. It shrinks in people who act out their dreams, a disorder that often comes before Parkinson's, so it could become an early warning.

stories.title: AI studies claiming fingerprints reveal blood type used mislabelled data, Australian researchers say
stories.summary: Lars Kooijman (Monash) and Stephanie Summersby (UNSW) traced several of over a dozen such papers to 6,000 fingerprints from 600 people that never came with blood types, and want them retracted. Elsevier and IEEE are investigating: a hype check for AI health claims.

stories.title: Australia passed a law making apps and AI chatbots protect users from serious harm
stories.summary: The Digital Duty of Care covers games, apps, social media and AI chatbots, with extra protections for under-18s, fines of up to 5% of global revenue or $109.2 million, and the right for people to take legal action. It takes effect 12 months after Royal Assent.

stories.title: The plastic in comic-book bags, stacked hundreds deep, could insulate moon bases
stories.summary: University of Pennsylvania engineers stacked hundreds of aluminium-coated Mylar films into flexible insulation that matched top vacuum insulators and kept working after 10 squeezes of about 91 kg on a fingertip's area, for a Moon that swings from 121°C to -133°C. Lab tests so far.

stories.title: A Georgia Tech robot with soft silicone thumbs grasped 23 of 25 blueberry clusters
stories.summary: Georgia Tech's CLASP harvester, from start-up Fructus Robotics, uses two cameras and a gripper whose silicone bands roll ripe berries off like a thumb, leaving unripe ones on the bush; in field trials on South Georgia farms it grasped 23 of 25 clusters on its own. Help for farms short of pickers.

stories.title: German start-up Q.ANT is piloting chips that run AI maths on light, to save power
stories.summary: Q.ANT's photonic co-processors work beside GPUs and are in a pilot at cloud firm IONOS, with more than 30 engineering teams building models for them, the company says. Light makes little heat, so the aim is to cut AI's energy and cooling bills.
